unit.title: Develop an understanding of concepts and application of optoelectronics technology

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain how an LED gives out light, and describe three ways to tell which lead is the anode and which is the cathode.
essays.modelAnswer: An LED is a diode made of a semiconductor material. When it is forward biased, with the anode more positive than the cathode, current flows across the junction inside the chip and energy is given out as light. The colour depends on the material used. When it is reverse biased it blocks the current and does not light. To find the leads: on a new LED the longer lead is the anode and the shorter lead is the cathode. The rim of a round LED has a flat edge on the cathode side. Inside the clear case the cathode is usually the larger, flag-shaped piece. You can also check with a multimeter on diode test: the LED glows faintly or shows about 1.6–2 V when the red lead is on the anode. The data sheet confirms the pin layout.
markingPoints: Semiconductor diode that gives out light when forward biased (current flows)
Blocks current and does not light when reversed
Longer lead is the anode
Flat edge on the rim marks the cathode
Multimeter diode test or data sheet (or larger flag inside) as a further check

essays.stem: A red LED needs about 2 V and 20 mA and is to be run from a 12 V bench supply. Explain, step by step, how you would work out and choose its series resistor, including its power rating.
essays.modelAnswer: First find the LED's forward voltage and current from the data sheet: here about 2 V and 20 mA (0.02 A). The resistor must drop the rest of the supply voltage, so 12 V − 2 V = 10 V across it. Using Ohm's law, R = V ÷ I = 10 ÷ 0.02 = 500 Ω. 500 Ω is not a common value, so I choose the next higher standard value, 560 Ω, so that the current is a little lower and safer, about 18 mA. Then I check the power: P = V × I = 10 × 0.018, which is about 0.18 W. A 0.25 W resistor would just do, but a 0.5 W resistor gives a safer margin and runs cooler. Finally I build the circuit with the supply off, and when the assessor switches on I measure the current to check it is close to what I worked out.
markingPoints: Uses the data sheet values for forward voltage and current
Voltage across resistor = 12 − 2 = 10 V
Chooses the next higher standard value (560 Ω)
Works out power (about 0.18–0.2 W) and picks a suitable rating with margin

essays.stem: Compare a light-dependent resistor (LDR), a photodiode and a phototransistor. Say how each responds to light and give one use for each.
essays.modelAnswer: An LDR is a resistor whose resistance falls as more light falls on it: it may be very high in the dark and only a few hundred ohms in bright light. It is cheap and simple but reacts slowly, so it suits jobs like a dusk-to-dawn switch on a street or security light. A photodiode is a diode, usually connected in reverse bias. When light falls on it, a small current flows, and this current rises with the light. It reacts very quickly, so it is used in fibre optic receivers and in light meters. A phototransistor works like a transistor switched on by light instead of by a base current. It gives a larger current than a photodiode for the same light but is slower. It is used in optocouplers, beam sensors on gates, and counting sensors on conveyors.
markingPoints: LDR: resistance falls as light rises; slow; used in dusk switches or similar
Photodiode: reverse biased, small current that rises with light
Photodiode is fast: fibre receivers, light meters or similar
Phototransistor: light acts like base current, gives more current than a photodiode
Phototransistor use: optocoupler, beam sensor, counter

essays.stem: Explain what an optocoupler is, how it works, and why it is used. Give one example from a control circuit.
essays.modelAnswer: An optocoupler, also called an opto-isolator, is a small package with an LED on one side and a light sensor, often a phototransistor, on the other. There is no wire between the two sides. When current flows through the LED it gives out light inside the package. The light falls on the sensor, which then lets current flow in the second circuit. So a signal passes across by light only. It is used to keep two circuits electrically apart. This protects a small, delicate control circuit from high voltages, electrical noise and faults in the circuit it controls, and it can protect the person using it. For example, a small controller working at 5 V can switch on a motor drive or a relay circuit at a higher voltage through an optocoupler, so that a fault on the motor side cannot reach the controller.
markingPoints: LED and light sensor in one package with no electrical connection
Current in the LED makes light that switches the sensor
Signal passes by light only
Keeps circuits apart: protects from high voltage, noise or faults
A sensible example, such as a low-voltage controller switching a higher-voltage circuit

essays.stem: Describe the safety precautions to follow when working with lasers and bright LED light sources.
essays.modelAnswer: Never look straight into a laser beam, a laser pointer or the end of a fibre that may carry laser light, and never point a laser at anyone. Some lasers give infrared light that cannot be seen, so the eye gets no warning. A laser can damage the eye in under a second. Read the warning label and class on the laser and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules. Switch the laser off when it is not in use, and aim beams at a dull, non-shiny stop so that they cannot reflect off mirrors, metal or watches. Use the right safety glasses where the Centre requires them. Very bright LEDs, such as those in floodlights, should not be stared at either; look at them from the side or use a diffuser. Keep all work at extra-low voltage from the bench supply, and report any damaged laser or eye injury at once.
markingPoints: Never look into a laser beam or a fibre end; never point a laser at people
Some lasers are infrared and invisible; damage can be very fast
Follow labels, the maker's instructions and Centre rules; switch off when not in use
Control reflections: aim at a dull stop, remove shiny items
Do not stare at bright LEDs; wear eye protection as required; report injuries

essays.stem: Describe how your group would safely build and test an LED circuit on a breadboard at the Centre, from planning to clean-up.
essays.modelAnswer: We start by drawing the circuit and reading the LED data sheet, then work out the resistor value and check it with the instructor. We collect the parts and check the resistor colour code with a meter. With the bench supply switched off, we build the circuit on the breadboard, with the LED the right way round, the longer lead to the positive side. We check the wiring against the drawing and ask the assessor to check it. The assessor then connects the bench supply at the agreed extra-low voltage, such as 9 V, and switches on. We measure the voltage across the LED and the resistor and the current, and record them in a table. If the LED does not light, we switch off, prove the board dead, and look for faults such as reversed polarity or a loose wire. At the end we switch off, take the circuit apart, return parts and put cut leads in a container.
markingPoints: Plans: draws the circuit, uses the data sheet, works out the resistor
Builds with the supply off and the LED polarity correct
Assessor checks the wiring and connects the extra-low-voltage supply
Measures and records voltage and current
Switches off before any change; finds faults; cleans up and returns parts

essays.stem: Explain how a solar cell produces electricity, and how cells are joined in a panel to give more voltage or more current.
essays.modelAnswer: A solar cell is a thin slice of semiconductor, usually silicon, with a junction inside it, like a large flat diode. When light falls on the cell, the energy of the light frees electrons in the material, and the junction pushes them one way. This is the photovoltaic effect. If a load is connected, a direct current flows. One silicon cell gives only about 0.5 to 0.6 V, and the current depends on the size of the cell and how bright the light is. To get a useful voltage, many cells are joined in series inside a panel, positive of one to negative of the next, so their voltages add up. To get more current, cells or whole panels are joined in parallel, positive to positive and negative to negative. Shade on even one cell in a series string can cut the output of the whole string.
markingPoints: Semiconductor junction; light frees electrons (photovoltaic effect)
Gives direct current to a connected load
One cell gives only about half a volt
Series connection adds voltages
Parallel connection adds current (shading point accepted as extra)

essays.stem: Explain the advantages of LED lighting over filament lamps, and describe two things an installer must take care of when fitting LED lighting.
essays.modelAnswer: LEDs turn much more of the electrical energy into light and much less into heat than filament lamps, so they use less power for the same light. This lowers the electricity bill, which matters for homes and businesses in Jamaica. LEDs last many times longer, so there are fewer lamp changes. They are tough because there is no glass bulb or filament to break, they light at once, and they come in many colours and shapes. They also give off less heat into the room. An installer must take care with a few things. LEDs work on low-voltage direct current, so they need a driver, and the driver must match the LEDs and the dimmer, if one is used. The polarity of DC connections must be right. The heat that is made must be carried away, so LEDs need a heat sink or good air flow, or they fail early.
markingPoints: More light for less power, so lower running cost
Much longer life; tough; instant on
Needs a matching driver (and a suitable dimmer)
Correct polarity on DC connections
Heat must be carried away (heat sink, air flow)

essays.stem: Describe how you would use a multimeter to test an LED and an LDR, and say how you would know if each one is faulty.
essays.modelAnswer: The parts are tested out of the circuit, or with the circuit switched off and proved dead. For the LED I set the meter to diode test. With the red lead on the anode and the black lead on the cathode, a good red LED shows about 1.6 to 2 V and may glow faintly. When I swap the leads it should show OL. If it shows OL both ways, the LED is open circuit. If it shows near zero both ways, it is short circuit. Either way it is faulty. For the LDR I set the meter to resistance. I cover the LDR with my hand or a black cap and read a high resistance, then shine a lamp on it and read a much lower value. If the reading does not change with the light, or shows OL or zero all the time, the LDR is faulty. I record all readings.
markingPoints: Tests with the part out of circuit or the circuit off and proved dead
LED on diode test: about 1.6–2 V forward (faint glow), OL reversed
OL both ways = open; near zero both ways = short
LDR on resistance: high in the dark, low in the light
No change with light = faulty; readings recorded

essays.stem: Describe five uses of optoelectronic devices in homes, businesses or industry in Jamaica, naming the device used in each.
essays.modelAnswer: In homes, a TV or air-conditioner remote control uses an infrared LED to send its signal, and a sensor in the set receives it. Street lights and security lights use a photocell or LDR to switch on at dusk and off at dawn. Shops and supermarkets use barcode scanners, which shine light on the stripes and read the reflection with a light sensor. Many homes, schools and businesses now have solar panels made of photovoltaic cells to cut electricity bills. Automatic gates and doors use an infrared beam and a phototransistor to detect a car or person in the way. Telephone and internet companies send data along fibre optic cables using laser or LED light and photodiode receivers. Factories use optocouplers in control panels, and light sensors to count goods on conveyors. Signs and displays use LEDs and seven-segment displays.
markingPoints: Each correct use with the right device named (1 mark each, up to 5)
e.g. remote control (IR LED), dusk switch (LDR/photocell), barcode scanner, solar panel (PV cells)
e.g. gate beam sensor (IR LED and phototransistor), fibre link (laser/photodiode)
e.g. optocoupler in a control panel, conveyor counter, LED signs and displays
Examples are set in homes, businesses or industry

practical1.title: Build and test LED indicator circuits in series and in parallel
practical1.brief: As a group, plan, build and test two LED circuits on a breadboard: (a) one red LED with its series resistor, and (b) three LEDs in parallel, each with its own resistor. Use the LED data sheets to work out each resistor for a 9 V supply, and have the instructor check your working before you build. Build everything with the supply off. The assessor checks your wiring, then connects the bench supply at 9 V DC and switches it on. No mains is used at any point. Each member works out at least one resistor, builds or wires one part, and takes and records at least one voltage or current reading. Fill in a results table showing the worked-out and measured values, and compare them. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the board is taken apart and the bench is clean.
materials: 5 mm LEDs (red, green and yellow) with their data sheets
Assorted resistors (for example 330 Ω, 390 Ω, 470 Ω, 560 Ω), 0.25 W or 0.5 W
Extra-low-voltage bench power supply, connected and switched by the assessor
Digital multimeter with test leads (checked before use)
photos: The circuit drawing and the resistor working-out sheet
Circuit (a) built on the breadboard with the supply off, LED polarity visible
Circuit (a) lit, with the meter reading the current
Circuit (b), three LEDs in parallel, lit
The bench cleared, parts returned and cut leads in a container
checklist: Read the data sheet and worked out a resistor value correctly
Chose a suitable standard resistor value and power rating
Built or wired a part of the circuit with the supply off
Put the LED the right way round
Set the meter correctly and took a voltage or current reading safely
Recorded readings in the table and compared them with the worked-out values
Switched off and asked the assessor before changing the circuit
Helped take the board apart and leave the bench clean
safety: Only the assessor connects and switches the bench supply; extra-low voltage only, never mains
Switch off before changing any part of the circuit
Do not look closely into bright LEDs; view them from the side
Cut leads are sharp: point them down when cutting and put them in a container

practical2.title: Build a light-activated switch and measure light sensors
practical2.brief: As a group, first measure a light-dependent resistor (LDR) with a multimeter in three light levels (covered, room light, under a lamp) and record the readings. Then build a dusk switch on a breadboard: the LDR and a resistor form a divider that drives a small NPN transistor, which switches an LED on when the LDR is covered. The instructor gives you the circuit drawing and part values. Build with the supply off. The assessor checks your wiring, then connects the bench supply at 6–9 V DC and switches on. No mains is used. Test the switch by covering and uncovering the LDR, and measure the voltage at the transistor base in light and dark. If the Centre has an optocoupler, also test it: drive its LED side from the circuit and show its output switching a second LED. Each member takes a reading, builds or checks part of the circuit, and explains one part of how it works to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Small general-purpose NPN transistor and its data sheet
LED and resistors as given on the instructor's drawing
Extra-low-voltage bench power supply, connected and switched by the assessor
Digital multimeter (checked before use), small desk lamp, black cap or card
photos: The LDR readings table for three light levels
The dusk switch built on the breadboard, supply off
The LED off with the LDR in light
The LED on with the LDR covered
The meter reading the base voltage
The optocoupler test, if done, and the cleared bench
checklist: Measured the LDR resistance on the right meter range and recorded it
Explained how LDR resistance changes with light
Built or checked part of the circuit against the drawing, with the supply off
Connected the transistor leads correctly from the data sheet
Tested the switch in light and dark and measured the base voltage
Explained one part of how the circuit works
Switched off before changes and helped clean up
safety: Only the assessor connects and switches the bench supply; extra-low voltage only
Switch off before changing the circuit
The desk lamp gets hot: do not touch the shade; keep it away from paper
Keep drinks away from the bench and equipment
